chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
title: Living alone above the club and landing the Orpheum Theatre pit job
summary: He lived alone upstairs at the club after the chef attacked the owner, then got a sick trumpeter's chair at the Orpheum Theatre pit and was hired on the spot.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Now, I lived way upstairs, there wasn't nobody in the hotel but me living. I couldn't understand that, but I was up there and I was sleeping, feeling good and the chef was kind of weird and he had them pretty women too and the boss

was named Stony, he was an Israeli man, so one night I had gone upstairs and gone to bed, and right next to the Big Apple was a synagogue and Willie the Lion, well, Willie the Lion and his brother, they were going to that synagogue, because Willie the Lion is a Catholic. His brother Melvin, the whole family, so now --

No, I met his brother, but he knew of me, Willie the Lion was a big man in New York. I hadn't made New York yet. I was over there. So while I was sleeping it seems as though that the man who owned the place had enraged the chef and the chef creased his head with a cleaver, so wasn't nobody in -- the doors were locked, but I could get out the back, you know, and I was in there by myself, and the chef had left was what necessary to be eaten and I stayed there about three months, and then I said, well, my goodness, I can't stay up here all the time. Grove Street was terrible, it was an awful street, but I knew everybody and Joe was back in there resting himself, playing cards and he said, don't worry about it. We got everything we need, but I found, I would have had to get into that circuit. So one day I went to the Orpheum Theatre and I'm lucky. That day the trumpet player got sick and didn't make it and I ran home and got my horn and got in that pit and they were playing all the numbers in the chorus, the chorus was playing all the numbers, that I mostly knew and I didn't have no not too many heavy strong pit music, and they didn't

let me play for the motion pictures, because had I played for the motion pictures, they would have got me. So I got in that pit and set that pit afire, got the job immediately so that was all right, and then I really started then (unintelligible) his name was Joe James, he's got a son, named Joe James also, he's a big man, so Joe taught me everything, trumpet, and they had a man named Clarence Adams, one of the greatest clarinets I've ever heard. He was from Winston-Salem, North Carolina and this I realized he said you look like a man I know and I said yeah, who, and he says John Adams. Plays trombone and he also plays mandolin and he owns a barber shop and he owns the busline and I said, yes, that's what he is.
